formula: I((math + read)/2) ~ I(students/teachers) + english + lunch + calworks + (1 | county)
notes: RULE GAP: the documented response is score = (math + read)/2, which is no column, so response names math, the formula holds the mean and read is ignored. Read CASchools.Rd and StockWatson2007.Rd: Stock and Watson (2007) fit lm(score ~ stratio + english + lunch + calworks) (Table 7.1, col. 5, the page's fmc5), stratio = students/teachers, with sandwich standard errors and no grouping. The 420 K-6 and K-8 districts repeat within California counties (county, a factor with many levels), so county is filed as the grouping factor, a cluster the source treats as independent; the random intercept is the reader's proposal. students and teachers enter the ratio, so both are covariates; district and school are ids; grades, computer, expenditure and income are not in this model. Hand check #162: the documented response is the average score, a response of the table computed from the row; the county intercept (45 counties of 1 to 29 districts) stays the reader's proposal.

formula: I(tmathssk + treadssk) ~ classk + totexpk + sex + freelunk + race + (1 | schidkn)
notes: Project STAR kindergarten, students in schools (schidkn, the school indicator). The help page cites Stock and Watson (2003), Introduction to Econometrics, chapter 11 (experiments and quasi-experiments), recalled, not read: the kindergarten differences estimates regress the student's total of the math and reading scaled scores on the class-type indicators (classk: small class, regular with aide), adding teacher experience (totexpk), school indicator variables, and sex, free-lunch eligibility and race. Schools enter as fixed effects, so the school is rendered as a random intercept and published_model is no. RULE GAP: the book's response is the sum tmathssk + treadssk, which is no column; response names tmathssk and the formula holds the sum. Hand check #162: one row models the documented sum, not each score (Stock and Watson, 3rd ed., Table 13.2, col. 4: 5,748 students, school indicators); 79 schools of 34 to 136 students.

formula: I(metafor::escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = exp_mean, m2i = con_mean, sd1i = exp_se * sqrt(exp_n), sd2i = con_se * sqrt(con_n), n1i = exp_n, n2i = con_n)$yi) ~ 1 + (1 | study_ID) + (1 | comp_ID)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.besson2016, examples: dat$sd_c <- con_se * sqrt(con_n); dat$sd_e <- exp_se * sqrt(exp_n); escalc(measure='SMD', m1i=exp_mean, m2i=con_mean, sd1i=sd_e, sd2i=sd_c, n1i=exp_n, n2i=con_n); mod1 <- rma.mv(yi ~ 1, V = vi, random = list(~ 1 | study_ID, ~ 1 | comp_ID)). The response names escalc's first input (the experimental group's mean), the formula's left side is the standardized mean difference (Hedges' g, escalc's call with its exact correction) as an expression of the columns, and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. 473 comparisons of offspring behaviour (anxiety, exploration, activity) after maternal diet manipulation in rodents, from 55 studies (study_ID); comp_ID is unique per row, so its term is effect-level. dam_ID and animal_ID index dam and offspring groups the model does not fit, con_ID shared controls. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Besson et al. (2016). Hand check #162: the effect size is a response of the table, computed from the row.

formula: I(log((waward / (wtotal - waward)) / (maward / (mtotal - maward)))) ~ type + (1 | study) + (1 | study:obs)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.bornmann2007, examples: escalc(measure='OR', ai=waward, n1i=wtotal, ci=maward, n2i=mtotal); res <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/obs) and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ type, random = ~ 1 | study/obs) (fellowship vs grant applications). The response names escalc's first input (women awarded), the formula's left side is the log odds ratio of an award for women vs men as an expression of the columns (escalc adds 1/2 only to tables with a zero cell), and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. 66 award comparisons from 21 studies; obs numbers them within study, so study:obs has one level per row and its term is effect-level. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel (2007), Journal of Informetrics. Hand check #162: the effect size is a response of the table, computed from the row; every cell of the 66 tables is positive, so no correction applies.

formula: I(log((lh.le + 0.5) * (rh.re + 0.5) / ((lh.re + 0.5) * (rh.le + 0.5)))) ~ 1 + (1 | study) + (1 | study:sample) + (1 | study:sample:sex)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size. Help page dat.bourassa1996, examples: escalc(measure='OR', ai=lh.le, bi=lh.re, ci=rh.le, di=rh.re, add=1/2, to='all'); rma(yi, vi, subset=sex=='combined'); rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/sample, subset=sex=='combined'); then the page keeps a sample's male and female rows where both are reported and its combined row otherwise and fits, filed here, rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/sample/sex) (a subset fit filed on the whole object: the 96 rows hold one combined row for each of the 54 samples and 21 male/female pairs). The response names escalc's first input (left-handed left-eyed), the formula's left side is the log odds ratio of handedness and eye dominance with the 1/2 correction, and response_type is the effect size's; confidence is medium for that reason only. Sample numbers are unique across the 47 studies; study:sample:sex has one level per row, so sex goes to ignore and its term stays in the formula. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Bourassa, McManus & Bryden (1996), Laterality. Hand check #162: the effect size is a response of the table, computed from the row; the 54 sample numbers are unique across the 47 studies, so sample is the nested factor.

formula: I(metafor::escalc(measure = "ROM", m1i = m1i, m2i = m2i, sd1i = sd1i, sd2i = sd2i, n1i = n1i, n2i = n2i)$yi) ~ 1 + (1 | paper) + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size; the response names escalc's first input (the elevated-CO2 mean plant mass) and the formula's left side is the log ratio of means as the page's escalc call computes it. Help page dat.curtis1998, examples: escalc(measure='ROM', m1i=m1i, sd1i=sd1i, n1i=n1i, m2i=m2i, sd2i=sd2i, n2i=n2i); rma(yi, vi, method='DL') and the same on the subsets xtrt=='FERT' & level=='LOW' and xtrt=='LIGHT' & level=='LOW': a random-effects model with one effect per row and no paper level, so published_model is no. 102 observations (id) of woody plant mass under elevated vs ambient CO2 from 29 papers that vary further treatments (xtrt, level), so paper is the grouping factor by the ruling on repeated clusters; the documentation numbers papers and observations, hence medium. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Hedges, Gurevitch & Curtis (1999), Ecology. Hand check #162: the effect size is a response of the table, computed from the row.

formula: I(metafor::escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = mt, m2i = mc, sd1i = sdt, sd2i = sdc, n1i = nt, n2i = nc)$yi) ~ 0 + outcome + (1 | study)
notes: RULE GAP: no column holds the effect size, and the long table mixes continuous outcomes (rnic1, rnic2, snic1, snic2: means and SDs) with binary ones (rngoal1, rngoal2, sngoal1, sngoal2: xt and xc of nt and nc). Help page dat.dagostino1998, examples: escalc SMD from mt, mc, sdt, sdc, nt, nc and escalc OR from xt, xc, nt, nc; rma(yi, vi) per outcome (one row per study each); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, obs=esid, rho=0.7) and rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, subset=outcome %in% c('rnic1','rnic2')) with no random effects (no noteworthy heterogeneity), so published_model is no. The filed row is the reader's: the standardized mean difference (Hedges' g, escalc's call; the response names its first input mt) per continuous outcome with a study intercept, the binary outcomes' rows leaving it missing. 72 rows, 8 outcomes per antihistamine trial (9 studies). The source weights each effect by its sampling (co)variance, which the formula leaves out. D'Agostino et al. (1998). Hand check #162: the effect size is a response of the table, computed from the row, for the continuous outcomes rnic1, rnic2, snic1 and snic2; mt is missing on the binary outcomes' 36 rows and on one row each of snic1 and snic2.

formula: cbind(exac, total - exac) ~ treatment + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.baker2009, examples: pw <- pairwise(treatment, exac, total, studlab = paste(study, year), sm = 'OR'); net <- netmeta(pw, common = FALSE, ref = 'plac'), a random-effects network meta-analysis on the pairwise log odds ratios, and the additive component model netcomb(net); neither is a mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. 94 arms (one row per arm) of 39 COPD trials (id, labeled by study and year); exac counts patients with one or more exacerbations out of total. Baker, Baker & Coleman (2009). Hand check #162: stands; 39 trials of 2 to 4 arms.

formula: cbind(stroke, total - stroke) ~ treatment + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.dogliotti2014, examples: pw <- pairwise(treat = treatment, n = total, event = stroke, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'); net <- netmeta(pw, ref = 'plac') and the Mantel-Haenszel netmetabin(pw, ref = 'plac'); neither is a mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. One row per arm of antithrombotic trials in non-valvular atrial fibrillation (id, labeled by study), strokes out of total. Dogliotti, Paolasso & Giugliano (2014). Hand check #162: stands; 20 trials of 2 or 3 arms.

formula: cbind(death, randomized - death) ~ treatment + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.dong2013, examples: pw <- pairwise(treatment, death, randomized, studlab = id, sm = 'OR'); net <- netmetabin(pw, ref = 'plac'), a Mantel-Haenszel common-effect network meta-analysis, with netsplit for inconsistency; no mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. 99 arms of trials of inhaled COPD medications (id), deaths out of randomized. Dong et al. (2013). Hand check #162: stands; 41 trials of 2 to 4 arms.

formula: cbind(death, n - death) ~ treatment + (1 | study)
notes: RULE GAP: an arm-based network meta-analysis table whose page fits only netmeta. Help page dat.gurusamy2011, examples: pw <- pairwise(treatment, death, n, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'); net.MH <- netmetabin(pw, ref = 'cont') and net.IV <- netmeta(pw, ref = 'cont'); no mixed model on this table, so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM with a trial intercept. One row per arm of trials of interventions to decrease blood loss in liver transplantation, deaths at 60 days out of n; the details note one study with zero events in both arms that every network analysis drops. Gurusamy et al. (2011), via Efthimiou et al. (2019). Hand check #162: stands; 14 trials of 2 or 3 arms.

formula: cbind(resp, n - resp) ~ 0 + factor(id) + int + (1 | id) + (1 | id:int)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treat = int, event = resp, n = n, studlab = paste(author, year), reference = 'plac', sm = 'OR') turns the arms into log odds ratios per comparison; netmeta(pw, reference.group = 'placebo', common = FALSE) fits a random-effects network meta-analysis, and netcomb an additive component NMA. netmeta's random-effects model is rma.mv's random = ~ comp | study with rho = 1/2 (the dat.senn2013 page fits both and attributes the difference to the tau estimator); the reader renders it on the arms as the arm-based model with fixed study effects and compound-symmetric arm effects, written as (1 | id) + (1 | id:int) with equal variances, id:int one arm per row. 93 trials of 2 to 4 arms (Linde et al. 2016, J Clin Epidemiol; Ruecker et al. 2020). int.long spells out int; author and year label the trial. Hand check #162: published_model no, since netmeta fits normal log odds ratios after pairwise(), a likelihood other than this binomial one; the formula is the reader's proposal.

formula: cbind(r, N - r) ~ 0 + factor(author) + treatment + (0 + I(as.numeric(treatment != "Placebo")) | author) + (0 + I(as.numeric(treatment != "Placebo")) | author:treatment)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treatment, event = r, n = N, studlab = author, sm = 'OR'); netmeta(pw) fits the common- and random-effects network meta-analysis. author:treatment is one arm per row. Three trials (Boyd 1997, Calverly 2003 with four arms, Celli 2003), so author has three levels. Woods, Hawkins and Scott (2010, BMC Med Res Methodol) fit a Bayesian NMA of these counts on the log-hazard scale. Hand check #162: the paper's Appendix B fits the counts by a binomial model with a complementary log-log link, fixed trial baselines and random contrasts of the active treatments, each of the two random terms with half the contrast variance, which the formula cannot state; the trial factor may keep three levels, since a documented model fits it. RULE GAP: the cloglog link is outside Family for a binomial response, so family is blank; the slope on the active-treatment indicator has no column, so random_slopes is blank and the formula holds it.

formula: diff ~ 0 + factor(study) + treatment + (1 | study) + (1 | study:treatment)
notes: Help page example: to.wide(dat, study='study', grp='treatment', ref='TAU', grpvars=c('diff','se','n')) turns these arms into contrasts yi = diff1 - diff2 against each study's TAU (or first) arm, vi = se1^2 + se2^2, V with the shared arm's covariance; rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + No.treatment + Wait.list + Placebo + F2F.CBT + Hybrid.CBT + Multimedia.CBT, random = ~ comp | study, rho=1/2). The reader renders the contrast model on this arm table as the arm-based model with fixed study effects (differencing removes them) and compound-symmetric arm effects, written as (1 | study) + (1 | study:treatment) with equal variances, as the dat.senn2013 page fits it on arms; study:treatment is one arm per row. Further fits: random inconsistency effects (list(~ comp | study, ~ comp | design)), the CBT forms collapsed, and a component NMA CBT:(multi + cog + ba + psed + home + prob + soc + relax + goal + final). diff is the arm's standardized mean change, se its standard error, which the source weights by; intensity = sessions x length. Lopez-Lopez et al. 2019, Psychol Med. Hand check #162: published_model no, since the arm rendering does not reproduce the contrast model: three comparisons of a treatment with itself carry heterogeneity there, while study:treatment effects cancel; the formula is the reader's proposal, the documented model rma.mv on the contrasts with their known sampling covariance.

formula: expenditures ~ revenues + grants + (1 | municipality)
notes: RULE GAP: the source's model is dynamic, each series regressed on lags of all three, which the registry cannot hold; the static equation on the contemporaneous revenues and grants is the reader's proposal, not a rendering of it. Read Municipalities.Rd: 265 Swedish municipalities, 1979-1987, Greene (2003) Table 18.2 (the page shows only summary()). Dahlberg and Johansson (2000, JAE 15, 401-416) estimate a trivariate dynamic panel model of expenditures, own-source revenues and grants by first-differenced GMM with bootstrapped critical values (abstract: one lag in the expenditures equation, no dynamics in the revenues and grants equations); no random effect. Panel ruling: municipality is the grouping factor with a random intercept. Only the expenditures equation is filed, since revenues and grants as responses would regress on the same three series. year is the panel time index. Hand check #162: 265 municipalities observed nine times each.

formula: log(wage) ~ weeks + south + smsa + married + experience + I(experience^2) + occupation + industry + union + gender + ethnicity + education + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: the documented model is Hausman-Taylor, a random-effects model estimated by instrumental variables (weeks, south, smsa, married, gender and ethnicity exogenous); the instruments are not representable, so the row is its random-intercept model. Read PSID7682.Rd: 595 PSID individuals, 1976-1982 (Cornwell and Rupert 1988). The page fits plm(log(wage) ~ weeks + south + smsa + married + experience + I(experience^2) + occupation + industry + union + gender + ethnicity + education | weeks + south + smsa + married + gender + ethnicity, model = "ht") (Baltagi and Khanti-Akom 1990, Table I, col. HT) and two variants with other exogenous sets and time dummies (Tables II and III). id indexes the individual; year is the time index. Same panel as stata_psidextract. Hand check #162: stands; a mixed-model fit does not reproduce the Hausman-Taylor estimates, which rest on the exogeneity assumptions; Table III's time dummies (psid_ht3) are the same model. 595 individuals over seven years.

formula: choice ~ brand intercept + disp.<brand> + feat.<brand> + price.<brand> (conditional logit over heinz41, heinz32, heinz28 and hunts32, one coefficient per attribute) + household-varying brand intercepts and attribute coefficients over id (random-coefficients logit)
notes: RULE GAP: Read the Ecdat page: repeated catsup purchases of households (id) with each brand's display, feature advertisement and price; the page gives no model. Its source, Jain, Vilcassim and Chintagunta (1994, JBES 12, 317-328), fits by its abstract (IDEAS/RePEc) a random-coefficients logit to household panel data, brand preferences and responses to marketing variables varying across households, the heterogeneity distribution approximated by a discrete distribution. Rendered as a categorical response with household random effects over id; the discrete heterogeneity and the alternative-specific attributes have no lme4 form. family blank: categorical responses are outside the contract's family rule. Hand check #162: stands; the household-varying coefficients act on each brand's columns, which random_slopes cannot name, so the formula states them in words.

formula: choice ~ brand intercept + disp.<brand> + feat.<brand> + price.<brand> (conditional logit over sunshine, kleebler, nabisco and private, one coefficient per attribute) + household-varying brand intercepts and attribute coefficients over id (random-coefficients logit)
notes: RULE GAP: Read the Ecdat page: repeated cracker purchases of households (id) with each brand's display, feature advertisement and price; the page gives no model. Its sources are Jain, Vilcassim and Chintagunta (1994, JBES 12, 317-328), whose abstract (IDEAS/RePEc) fits a random-coefficients logit to household panel data, brand preferences and responses to marketing variables varying across households with a discrete heterogeneity distribution, and Paap and Franses (2000), a dynamic multinomial probit. Rendered as a categorical response with household random effects over id; the discrete heterogeneity and the alternative-specific attributes have no lme4 form. family blank: categorical responses are outside the contract's family rule. Hand check #162: stands; the household-varying coefficients act on each brand's columns, which random_slopes cannot name, so the formula states them in words. Paap and Franses's (2000) dynamic multinomial probit has the same response and grouping, so it files no row.

formula: choice ~ brand intercepts + feat.<brand> + price.<brand> (conditional logit, one feature and one price coefficient across the four brands) + household random coefficients on the brand intercepts, feature and price by id (discrete support points)
notes: Jain, Vilcassim and Chintagunta (1994), JBES 12(3), 317-28, cited by the help page, abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc: A Random-Coefficients Logit Brand-Choice Model Applied to Panel Data, households differing in brand preferences and in their responses to marketing variables, the unknown heterogeneity distribution approximated by a discrete distribution. id the household making repeated purchases, choice the brand bought among four, feat.<brand> and price.<brand> each brand's newspaper feature and price. RULE GAP: a multinomial (conditional) logit is outside Family, so family is blank; the random coefficients have discrete support points rather than a normal distribution, rendered as household random effects. The same purchases in long form are rabe_hesketh yogurt.dta, where Rabe-Hesketh and Skrondal fit a mixed logit with correlated household brand effects. Hand check #162: stands; the household-varying coefficients act on each brand's columns, which random_slopes cannot name, so the formula states them in words. Rabe-Hesketh and Skrondal's three mixed logits (ch12.do, section 12.7, Hiland left out) have the same response and grouping, so they file no row.

formula: Ketchup.choice ~ brand intercepts + log(price.<brand>) (conditional logit over heinz, hunts, delmonte and stb) + a household-varying log-price coefficient (reflected lognormal) and a two-point Heinz-versus-other loyalty shifter over Ketchup.hid
notes: RULE GAP: Read the Ecdat page: ketchup purchases of households with each brand's price; the loaded columns are named Ketchup.hid, Ketchup.id and Ketchup.choice, and Ketchup.id is the purchase index within the household; the page gives no model. Its source, Kim, Blattberg and Rossi (1995, JBES 13, 291-303), fits by its abstract (IDEAS/RePEc) a random coefficient logit whose brand-level intercepts and price slopes vary across households, on household panel data of two product categories, and tests the parametric heterogeneity distribution against semiparametric density estimates. Rendered as a categorical response with household random effects over Ketchup.hid; the price slope on alternative-specific prices has no lme4 form, so random_slopes stays blank. family blank: categorical responses are outside the contract's family rule. Hand check #162: the paper (sections 1 and 2, Table 6) takes log prices, a reflected lognormal price coefficient and an independent two-point loyalty shifter for Heinz against the others, not normal brand intercepts; it analyzes these 4,956 purchases of 1,956 households.

formula: log(length) ~ 1 + (1 | year)
notes: RESPONSE INFERRED: no model is fitted in the source. Help page: periods between rain events at Winnipeg International Airport, length 'the length of time from the completion of the last rain event to the beginning of the next rain event' in days, year the calendar year; the examples draw boxplot(length ~ year) and boxplot(log(length) ~ year) and fit no model, and the year grouping is inferred from those boxplots. RULE GAP: one station's record, read as dry spells grouped by year (many events per year, as a sampling month groups squid) rather than as a time series without replication. Hand check #162: 21 years of 56 to 141 spells each.
